“Good afternoon, Councilors. My name is Chula
Phillips and I live with my husband Gary Phillips
at 13603 NE 50th Avenue in the Pleasant Valley
area.

I am speaking today to formally oppose the
proposed rezoning of the tract in our
neighborhood from R1-7.5 to R32 and R36.
Like many of my neighbors, I chose to invest my
life, my future, and my hard-earned savings into
Pleasant Valley precisely because of its unique
character. We moved here for the quality of
life—because it is quiet, less congested, and
purposefully insulated from heavy commercial
activity.
This proposed plan completely disregards that
identity. By dropping multi-story, high-density
multifamily zoning directly into a perimeter
completely surrounded by single-family homes,
this council is effectively forcing an urban, city-
like environment onto a semi-rural
neighborhood overnight.
 If passed, this rezone will result in an
immediate, staggering population spike of up to
500% on a single piece of land.
Under Washington’s Growth Management Act,
growth is not allowed to outpace infrastructure.
This is the law of concurrency. Yet, this plan
contains no funded, viable strategy to expand
public infrastructure to match this sudden
density.
To prove this, I have submitted an extensive
research and data packet for the official record
today. I urge you to look closely at the data I
provided, which demonstrates three critical
failures this rezone will cause:
   1.    Traffic gridlock: Our local intersections
     and narrow semi-rural roads lack the
     capacity to absorb this massive influx of
     vehicles, creating immediate safety risks.
   2.    School overcrowding: The local school
     district lacks the physical space and budget
     to handle a sudden 500% population spike,
     directly harming our children’s education.
   3.    Infrastructure strain: The severe lack of
     neighborhood parking and public utilities
    means local quality of life will collapse
    under the weight of this incompatible
    design.
We understand the county faces state housing
targets, but meeting those quotas by destroying
established, quiet communities is bad planning
and legally vulnerable. Please protect the
integrity of Pleasant Valley. I urge you to deny
the R32/R36 designation and preserve our R1-
7.5 zoning.

Thank you
I appreciate your consideration."

Dear Clark County Community Planning Team,

I am writing regarding the postcards mailed in August and September announcing public
meetings for the Clark 2045 Growth Management Plan Update. I reviewed both postcards
carefully, including the QR code and the web addresses provided. Despite this, I was unable to
locate the Preferred Alternative Map or any supporting documents that would allow
residents to understand the proposals under consideration.

In recent days, some residents have circulated informal descriptions of potential zoning
changes in the area south of NE 139th Street. These descriptions include significant upzoning,
reduced parking requirements, and land‑use changes tied to industrial development. I have not
been able to find any official County materials that confirm or explain these ideas.

I was also unable to locate information regarding traffic impacts, infrastructure capacity,
school impacts, or parking requirements—all of which are essential components of any
substantial land‑use change under the Growth Management Act and SEPA. While some of this
information may exist within the EIS or other technical documents, these materials alone are
not sufficient for the public to understand the implications of the Preferred Alternative without
clear, accessible explanations. Most residents are not professional planners and do not have
staff or consultants to interpret specialized land‑use documents and language. For meaningful
public participation to occur, the County must provide the Preferred Alternative Map and
accompanying plain‑language descriptions of how any proposed changes would affect our
neighborhood.

As noted above, I have been unable to locate the Preferred Alternative Map or the supporting
materials needed to provide informed input. It is possible that some of these documents exist
somewhere on the County’s website and that I simply did not see them. If so, I would
appreciate being directed to the specific locations of the following: •Parking requirement
information • Infrastructure capacity analysis (including stormwater, flooding, water supply,
and sewer system impacts) • Emergency services capacity evaluation • Environmental and
habitat impact information • Evaluation of how proposed building height, scale, and density
would transition to adjacent existing development patterns • Economic and fiscal impact
analysis

We are particularly interested in these materials as they describe how the plan would impact
the Heights at Pleasant Valley (roughly between 50th and 72nd Ave and North of 139th St to
146th St.).

Clear and timely access to these materials is essential for residents to understand the proposals
and participate meaningfully in the upcoming hearing.

The September postcard states that the County Council will take public testimony and make a
final decision on October 1 (continuing October 2 if necessary). Because we have been
unable to locate the Preferred Alternative Map or the supporting analyses, it is not possible for
residents to prepare informed comments before a final decision is made. Proceeding without
ensuring that residents have access to these materials would limit meaningful public
participation.

For these reasons, I respectfully request that the County postpone any final
decision until the Preferred Alternative Map and supporting documents have been
released and the public has had adequate time to review them.

To prepare for the October 1 meeting, I also request that the Preferred Alternative Map, any
proposed zoning changes, and all related supporting documents be sent to me electronically as
soon as possible.

Thank you for your attention to this matter and for supporting transparent public engagement.

Sincerely,

Michael Eyster

14007 NE 52nd Ave Vancouver, WA 98686

over of agricultural and green space and have seen 72nd avenue, 179th street, and 199th streets,

agricultural land. We have experience increase flooding over 209th street caused by wetland
destruction in the process of home building. Moreover, we are very tired of hearing about building
"affordable" housing to deal with the un-housed county population, when builders get tax breaks
for "affordable" homes that start at $350,000 or a very few studio apartments in a large complex
that require a monthly rent of $1800. We urge you to develop policies designed to build up rather
than out and stick with the current urban growth boundaries. We urge the Council to limit urban
growth boundary expansion, to protect agricultural lands, and to ambitiously address greenhouse
gas emissions reduction targets, aligned with the city of Vancouver's Climate Action Framework
and in line with the Clark County Public Health Climate Action Program.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This Transportation Impact Study (TIS) has been prepared in support of the proposed Skyview Station
development located at the northeast corner of the NE 139th Street/NE 10th Avenue intersection in Clark
County, Washington.

Project Description
▪             The proposed Skyview Station development will include approximately 80,150 square feet (SF) of
              shopping center with eight (8) buildings platted on separate lots. Two site accesses are proposed:
              □             A full-movement driveway is proposed on NE 10th Avenue, a designated collector street.
                            This driveway will be located opposite NE 141st Street and will include one inbound and
                            two outbound travel lanes.
              □             A second limited access driveway is proposed on NE 139th Street, a designated minor
                            arterial. This driveway will be limited to right-in/right-out (RIRO) movements only and will
                            be aligned nearly opposite the bus-only access serving the Salmon Creek Park & Ride. (A
                            technical road modification (TRM) will be submitted with the development application to
                            add the site driveway on NE 139th Street).
▪             The site has a covenant of record (AFN 5170404) that requires certain mitigation measures to be
              in place prior to issuance of a building permit; however, a concurrent process is underway to
              release all the identified measures based on an updated traffic analysis that demonstrates agency
              operational standards are met without mitigation.

Existing Conditions
▪             The site is within the City of Vancouver Urban Growth Area but outside City limits. Clark County
              zoning is General Commercial (GC).
▪             The arterial network surrounding the site includes NE 139th Street and NE 10th Avenue. Other
              major streets include NE Tenney Road, NE 134th Street, and NE 20th Avenue. Freeway access (I-5
              and I-205) is available from both NE 139th Street and NE 134th Street.
▪             All streets providing direct access to the site have sidewalks on both sides of the street with one
              exception: NE 139th Street does not have sidewalks on the north side of the street between
              NE 10th Avenue and NE 20th Avenue. WSDOT did not construct sidewalks on the north side of
              NE 139th Street as it crosses over the freeway and the segment along the site frontage does not
              currently have sidewalks.
▪             All streets providing direct access to the site have bike lanes on both sides of the street.
▪             C-TRAN has three bus routes that serve the project site. Two routes stop at the Salmon Creek
              Park & Ride station on the south side of NE 139th Street, across from the project site; and one
              stops on NE 139th Street just west of NE 10th Avenue.
▪             Turning movement counts for study area intersections were collected in either April or October
              2018.Five years of historical crash data did not show significant patterns or unexpected behaviors
              in the study area intersection.
▪             All study area intersections currently meet agency standards.




\\grp.mck\data\users\rlb\PIM Working Files\deltekpim.mcknze.com\RPT-Clark County-Skyview Station TIS-180917 REV.docx   1
▪             Traffic simulations indicate 95th percentile queues exceed available storage during the AM and/or
              PM peak hour at some intersections. None of these queues are expected to affect upstream
              intersection operations.
▪             All roadway segments currently meet the County’s capacity standard of 0.90 or better.

Pre-Development Conditions
▪             Two Clark County projects along NE 10th Avenue will fully connect NE 139th Street to NE 179th
              Street creating a local parallel route to I-5 on the west side of the freeway. Both are fully funded,
              and construction is expected to be nearly complete by the opening year of Skyview Station;
              therefore, these projects are included in the pre-development conditions.
▪             An average 2% annual growth rate was applied to existing 2018 traffic volumes over two (2) years
              to estimate 2020 background traffic growth. Figure 5 presented the AM and PM peak hour
              background traffic growth.
▪             In-process traffic volumes for four (4) projects were provided by Clark County staff.
▪             Near-term traffic reroutes based on the 2018 existing traffic counts were developed to account
              for the completion of the NE 10th Avenue connection between NE 139th Street to NE 179th
              Street.
▪             All study area intersections currently meet agency standards.
▪             Traffic simulations indicate 95th percentile queues exceed available storage during the AM and/or
              PM peak hour at some intersections. None of these queues are expected to affect upstream
              intersection operations.
▪             All roadway segments are anticipated to meet the County’s capacity standard of 0.90 or better,
              except for two segments:
              □             During the AM peak hour, the segment of NE Salmon Creek Avenue between NE 134th
                            Street and NE 50th Avenue is anticipated to have a v/c ratio of 1.08 in the eastbound
                            direction under pre-development conditions.
              □             During the PM peak hour, the segment of N 139th Street between the I-205 NB On-Ramp
                            and NE 20th Avenue is anticipated to have a v/c ratio of 0.91 in the westbound direction
                            under pre-development conditions.

Site Development
▪             The site comprises two tax lots (property identification numbers 185726000 and 185727000)
              totaling 8.66 acres. Both lots have existing development, a single-family home, and DeWitt
              Construction, but neither will remain with the Skyview Station development.
▪             Trip generation estimates were developed using the Institute of Transportation Engineers (ITE)
              Trip Generation Manual, 10th Edition. The pass-by trip rates are based on the ITE Trip Generation
              Handbook, 3rd Edition. The Shopping Center land use was used.
▪             Net site trip generation is anticipated at 180 AM peak hour, 454 PM peak hour and 5,072 daily
              trips. Of the total trips, 114 AM peak hour, 296 PM peak hour, and 3,312 daily trips are primary
              trips.
▪             Distribution for pass-by trips were estimated from the traffic count data at the intersection of
              NE 139th Street and NE 10th Avenue.


\\grp.mck\data\users\rlb\PIM Working Files\deltekpim.mcknze.com\RPT-Clark County-Skyview Station TIS-180917 REV.docx   2
▪             Site trip distribution for primary trips is based on the select zone base year (2010) and future year
              (2035) travel volumes plots for Traffic Analysis Zone (TAZ) 95.
▪             A site access is proposed on NE 139th Street with turns limited to right-in/right-out movements.
              A TRM is required to approve this access; therefore, this TIA addresses three access alternatives:
              1) No access, 2) Right-in only, and 3) Right-in/right out.

Site Access and Circulation
▪             Site-generated traffic volumes meet the criterial for allowing an additional driveway on a minor
              arterial, which supports the proposal for a right-in/right-out access on NE 139th Street.
▪             Both proposed accesses would meet the County spacing standards.
▪             NE 10th Avenue is a straight roadway with clear stopping and intersection sight distance in both
              directions as measured 15 feet from the edge of the vehicle travel lane. Landscaping along the
              site frontage will maintain the necessary sight triangles.
▪             NE 139th Street has a slight curvature but the proposed right-out movement from the site will
              have clear stopping and intersection sight distance looking to the west, as needed.
▪             Internal drive aisles will be constructed through the site connecting both the main driveway and
              proposed RIRO with all parcels on the site. All site parking will be accessible via the drive aisles
              and will have access to both proposed driveways.
▪             Pedestrians will have two site access connections from NE 139th Street and one connection from
              NE 10th Avenue.
▪             If access on NE 139th Street is restricted to right-in movements only, traffic would have two
              options for entering the site but only one option for exiting the site.
▪             If no access is provided on NE 139th Street, then all entering and exiting traffic would be
              concentrated at a single access point.

Post-Development Conditions
▪             All intersections currently meet agency standards and will continue to meet standards through
              the year 2020 with one exception. At the site access on NE 10th Avenue, the westbound left-turn
              movement will exceed capacity under post-development conditions.
▪             The addition of an access on NE 139th Street measurably improves the site access operations at
              NE 10th Avenue with either access alternative.
▪             Two county intersections will have queues that exceed available storage:
              □             Simulations show the westbound approach to NE 10th Avenue from the site is expected
                            to fail under post-development conditions generating substantial queues within the site.
              □             Simulations show several approaches at the NE 139th Street/NE 10 Avenue intersection
                            would have two approaches that exceed available storage under at least one scenario,
                            but the approach queues are not anticipated to affect upstream intersection operations.
▪             The westbound approach to NE 10th Avenue from the site is expected to have long queues in the
              site under post-development conditions. The addition of right-in only on NE 139th Street will
              shorten the queues but there would still be 13-14 queuing to turn left during the PM peak hour.
              The PM queues would shorten to 7-8 vehicles by adding the RIRO.


\\grp.mck\data\users\rlb\PIM Working Files\deltekpim.mcknze.com\RPT-Clark County-Skyview Station TIS-180917 REV.docx   3
▪             With the proposed RIRO access on NE 139th Street, the southbound approach shows short
              queues, which confirms that queuing on NE 139th Street will have minimal effect on the proposed
              site access.
▪             All roadway segments are anticipated to meet the County’s capacity standard of 0.90 or better
              except for two segments, but neither segment listed above reflects a project impact that would
              trigger the need for mitigation:
              □             On NE Salmon Creek Avenue between NE 134th Street and NE 50th Avenue, the segment
                            is over capacity under pre-development conditions and the proposed project does not
                            change the v/c ratio of the link.
              □             On NE 139th Street between the I-205 NB On-Ramp and NE 20th Avenue, the arterial
                            capacity assumption underestimates the capacity of this free-flow segment and capacity
                            of the adjacent segment is well below the County’s v/c ratio threshold.

Recommendations
▪             To address poor operations and queuing, a traffic signal is recommended at the intersection of
              NE 141st Street/Site Access/NE 10th Avenue with development of Skyview Station. A preliminary
              review of peak hour signal warrants shows that the PM peak hour would meet the warrant
              threshold.
▪             The proposed RIRO access on NE 139th Street is recommended for the following reasons:
              □             Site trip generation meets the County criteria for an additional driveway on a minor
                            arterial.
              □             The proposed location of the access on NE 139th Street will meet the driveway spacing
                            criteria for arterials.
              □             NE 139th Street is the only practical location for a second site access. A second access on
                            NE 10th Avenue would provide no operational benefits to either the site or the
                            surrounding transportation system.
              □             If no additional access is provided on NE 139th Street, then all entering and exiting traffic
                            would be concentrated at a single access point. Should circumstances arise, such as a
                            severe crash on NE 10th Avenue that interferes with the operations of the primary site
                            access, no other access options would be available.
              □             The RIRO provides additional access for emergency vehicles entering/exiting the site.
              □             Both the right-in and RIRO will reduce site traffic through the adjacent signalized
                            intersection at NE 139th Street and NE 10th Avenue, but the RIRO provides a greater
                            reduction to traffic on NE 10th Avenue.
              □             Both the right-in and RIRO improve operations at intersections adjacent to the site, but
                            the RIRO provides an overall greater benefit by more substantially reducing traffic
                            demand on NE 10th Avenue and the full site access opposite NE 141st Street.
              □             Both the right-in and RIRO reduce some queues at intersections adjacent to the site, but
                            the RIRO provides an overall greater benefit by reducing traffic demand at the full site
                            access opposite NE 141st Street.

I.            INTRODUCTION

This Transportation Impact Study (TIS) has been prepared in support of the proposed Skyview Station
development located at the northeast corner of the NE 139th Street/NE 10th Avenue intersection in Clark
County, Washington. Figure 1 in Appendix A presents a vicinity map indicating the project location.

Project Description

The proposed Skyview Station development will include approximately 80,150 square feet (SF) of
shopping center with eight (8) buildings platted on separate lots. As shown in the site plan in Figure 2, two
site accesses are proposed:
▪             A full-movement driveway is proposed on NE 10th Avenue, a designated collector street. This
              driveway will be located opposite NE 141st Street and will include one inbound and two outbound
              travel lanes.
▪             A second limited access driveway is proposed on NE 139th Street, a designated minor arterial.
              This driveway will be limited to right-in/right-out (RIRO) movements only and will be aligned
              nearly opposite the bus-only access serving the Salmon Creek Park & Ride.

A technical road modification (TRM) will be submitted with the development application to add the site
driveway on NE 139th Street. Per Clark County Code (CCC) Table 40.350.030-6, an additional driveway
may be allowed on a minor arterial for sites generating more than 2,000 daily trips. The access will meet
the driveway spacing criteria for arterials as outlined in CCC Table 40.350.030-4. However, because the
proposed RIRO has not been approved, traffic operations will be evaluated both with and without it.

The site has a covenant of record (AFN 5170404) that requires certain mitigation measures to be in place
prior to issuance of a building permit; however, a concurrent process is underway to release all the
identified measures based on an updated traffic analysis that reflects changes in assumptions about the
developable area, background growth rates, new network connections, and additional site access
consistent with those presented in this TIS. The update demonstrates that the transportation network can
meet agency operational standards with site development under current zoning regulations without
mitigation.

Scope of Analysis

This TIS has been prepared in accordance with Clark County Code (CCC) Section 40.350.020(D), as well as
pre-application notes provided by County staff dated June 7, 2018. The study includes a summary of
existing traffic conditions, crash review, proposed trip generation, and an analysis of intersection
operations, site accesses, and queuing.

The study parameters and areas of concern have been discussed with County staff as the project has
developed. A formal scoping letter was submitted August 13, 2018. (See Appendix B for documentation.)

Study Area

Clark County requires a TIS for proposed developments anticipated to generate more than 10 peak period
vehicle trips. Per CCC 40.350.020(D)(5), the study area may include intersections within three (3) miles of
the project site since trip generation is estimated greater than 250 new peak hour trips (i.e., primary trips).

 The existing conditions analysis is based on a current year 2018 inventory of transportation facilities and
 2018 traffic data.

 Site Conditions

 The site comprises two tax lots (property identification numbers 185726000 and 185727000) totaling 8.66
 acres. Both lots have existing development, a single-family home, and DeWitt Construction, but neither
 will remain with the Skyview Station development.

 The site is within the City of Vancouver Urban Growth Area but outside city limits. Clark County zoning is
 General Commercial (GC).

 Transportation System Inventory

 The transportation system was reviewed to identify the characteristics of the network serving the site.

 Vehicular Transportation Facilities

 Table 1 summarizes the characteristics of the study area roadways.

 Pedestrian Facilities

 All streets providing direct access to the site have sidewalks on both sides of the street with one exception:
 NE 139th Street does not have sidewalks on the north side of the street between NE 10th Avenue and
 NE 20th Avenue. WSDOT did not construct sidewalks on the north side of NE 139th Street as it crosses
 over the freeway and the segment along the site frontage does not currently have sidewalks.

 Bicycle Facilities

 All streets providing direct access to the site have bike lanes on both sides of the street.

 Transit Facilities

 C-TRAN has three bus routes that serve the project site. Two routes stop at the Salmon Creek Park & Ride
 station on the south side of NE 139th Street, across from the project site, and one stops on NE 139th
 Street just west of NE 10th Avenue. Buses enter and exit the Park & Ride from NE 139th Street, but other
 vehicles access the parking lot via NE 136th Street just east of the roundabout on NE 10th Avenue.

 Route #9 – Felida travels through the Felida neighborhood connecting the Salmon Creek Park & Ride with
 the 99th Street Transit Center. This route does not actually enter the Park & Ride but stops on the south
 side on NE 139th Street at NE 10th Avenue just across the intersection from the transit center. The route
 travels eastbound on NE 139th Street, loops around the Fred Meyer Shopping Center on NE 10th Avenue
 and NE Tenney Road, then returns westbound on NE 139th Avenue. Weekday service has hourly
 headways with the first bus departing at 6:27 AM and the last bus departing at 6:27 PM. Saturday service
 also has hourly headways with the first but departing at 9:22 AM and the last bus departing at 6:22 PM.
 The route does not run on Sundays.

 Route #105 – I-5 Express travels to/from downtown Portland via I-5 with interim stops at the 99th Street
 Transit Center and downtown Vancouver. Weekday southbound service begins at 6:00 AM and the final
 bus departs at 6:44 PM. Headways are as short as 20 minutes in the early morning to about 50 minutes
 midday and about 30 minutes during the evenings. The first northbound bus arrives at 6:37 AM and the
 last arrives at 8:06 PM. Headways vary from 25 minutes during peak commute periods to 55 minutes
 midday. There is no weekend service.

The NE 139th Street intersection with the I-5 northbound off-ramp had the greatest number of crashes.
Most crashes reported were turning collisions involving a vehicle making from the ramp making a
northbound left and a vehicle traveling eastbound or westbound on NE 139th Street. Note, this
intersection was not open until midway through 2014.

The NE 139th Street intersection with NE 20th Avenue had the second greatest number of crashes. Most
crashes reported were rear end collisions.

No crashes resulted in a fatality, but two crashes were reported as “suspected serious injury.” Both
occurred at the NE 139th Street/NE 20th Avenue intersection. One was reported in 2016 and involved a
bicyclist that was hit by a vehicle traveling eastbound on NE 139th Street. The other was a fixed-object
collision involving a driver traveling northbound on NE 20th Avenue who fell asleep.

Only one (1) pedestrian-related crash was reported at any of the study area intersections. It was reported
at the I-5 northbound off-ramp at NE 139th Street. A northbound vehicle turning right from the ramp
struck a pedestrian on NE 139th Street. A possible injury was indicated.




\\grp.mck\data\users\rlb\PIM Working Files\deltekpim.mcknze.com\RPT-Clark County-Skyview Station TIS-180917 REV.docx                                11
Intersection Crash Rates

When evaluating the relative safety of an intersection, consideration is given not only to the total number
and types of crashes occurring, but also to the number of vehicles entering the intersection. This concept,
referred to as a “crash rate,” is usually expressed in terms of the number of crashes occurring per one
million entering vehicles (MEV) for the intersection per year. Intersections having a crash rate higher than
1.0 crashes/MEV should be reviewed for opportunities to improve safety.

The intersection crash rate is calculated by dividing the average number of crashes per year by the MEV
per year. A daily traffic volume was estimated by dividing the PM peak hour volume at each intersection
by a peak-to-daily factor, or k-factor. A k-factor of 0.09 was derived using recent average daily traffic (ADT)
and PM peak hour volumes for several of the arterials obtained from the Southwest Washington Regional
Transportation Council (RTC) traffic database. This factor was applied to all study area intersections to
estimate ADT. Only 3.5 years was used in the crash rate calculations for the I-5 ramp intersections because
the interchange opened mid-year 2014.

III.          PRE-DEVELOPMENT CONDITIONS

The pre-development conditions reflect a build-out year scenario without the proposed development.
This scenario includes traffic from 2018 existing conditions, background traffic growth to year 2020, in-
process traffic from other approved developments that have not yet been constructed, and traffic
reroutes from changes in the transportation network.

Planned Transportation Improvements

The adopted 2018-2023 Clark County Transportation Improvement Program (TIP) were reviewed for
scheduled transportation projects within the study area that may affect intersection and/or roadway
capacity. The following improvements are identified in the study area:
▪             Project A: NE 10th Avenue – NE 149th Street to NE 154th Street
              □       Construct a 2-lane collector with center turn lane, bike lanes, and sidewalks.
              □       Project is fully funded with a cost of $11,535,000.
              □       Design is underway, and construction is scheduled for 2020-2021.
▪             Project B: NE 10th Avenue – NE 154th Street to NE 164th Street
              □       Construct a bridge over Whipple Creek and 2-lane collector with center turn lane, bike
                      lanes, and sidewalks.
              □       Project is fully funded with a cost of $23,213,000.
              □       Project is currently under construction and scheduled for completion in 2018-2019.
▪             Project 3: I-5/NE 179th Street – NE Delfel Road to NE 15th Avenue
              □       Improve roadway to a standard arterial (widening lanes and shoulders, installing bike
                      lanes and sidewalks, addressing mitigation). Possibly reconfigure the on-ramps/off-
                      ramps. Realign NE Delfel Road. Roundabouts, signal or intersection improvements will be
                      completed as part of this project.
              □       Project cost is estimated at $27,367,000 and is partially funded through 2022-2023.
              □       Planning and scoping is underway in partnership with WSDOT.
              □       Project may be accelerated if funding permits.
▪             Project 6: NE 15th Avenue – NE 179th Street to NE 10th Avenue
              □       Construct a 3-lane minor arterial including center turn lane/median, sidewalks, and
                      bicycle lanes.
              □       Project cost is estimated at $15,000,000 and is partially funded through 2022-2023.
              □       Scoping and traffic modeling is underway.
              □       Project may be accelerated if funding permits.

Both Project A and Project B are fully funded, and construction is expected to be nearly complete by the
opening year of Skyview Station; therefore, these projects are included in the pre-development
conditions.

The other two projects at the NE 179th Street interchange are not fully funded, and no improvements are
assumed for the future conditions in this TIS.

Background Traffic Growth

Background traffic growth is applied to existing traffic volumes to forecast future traffic demand. An
average 2% annual growth rate was applied to existing 2018 traffic volumes over two (2) years to estimate
2020 background traffic growth. Figure 5 presented the AM and PM peak hour background traffic growth.

In-Process Traffic

In-process traffic volumes account for developments that have been approved or that are under
construction at the time of a traffic study. These traffic volumes account for traffic that will be added to
the external road network before build-out of the proposed development occurs.

Traffic volumes for the following developments, as provided by Clark County staff, were included as
in-process:
▪             Vancouver Clinic at Salmon Creek
▪             Phase 1: 179th Street Commercial
▪             Phase 2: 179th Street Commercial
▪             iTech Preparatory School

Figure 6 presents the in-process traffic volumes for the AM and PM peak hours. Appendix F includes the
supporting documentation for all in-process developments.

Traffic Reroutes

The two Clark County TIP projects along NE 10th Avenue will fully connect NE 139th Street to NE 179th
Street, creating a local parallel route to I-5 on the west side of the freeway. This improvement is
anticipated to change some of the area travel patterns when completed.

A Transportation Impact Discipline Report for the NE 10 Avenue (NE 154th to NE 164th Street) Project
#370922 was prepared by Kittelson & Associates, Inc. in June 2014. The report included analysis of No
Build and Build conditions for an opening year (2018) and a future year of 2035. Because the traffic data
was collected prior to the opening of the NE 139th Street interchange, the opening year analysis needed
to estimate changes in travel patterns from the interchange improvements as well as the NE 10th Avenue
Project. Furthermore, the study only includes PM peak hour volumes and did not address many of the
intersections included the Skyview Station study area; therefore, this TIS estimated the near-term traffic
reroutes based on the 2018 existing traffic counts.

The NE 10th Avenue connection has the immediate potential to change three patterns of traffic flow:
▪             The NE 10th Avenue connection may provide a more direct route for to/from NE 179th Street
              than NW 11th Avenue. To estimate the rerouted traffic demand, approximately 20% of the traffic
              traveling east-west on NE 179th Street at NE Delfel Road was assumed to divert from NW 11th
              Avenue to NE 10th Avenue. This assumption diverts in 55 AM peak hour trips (35 northbound/20
              southbound) and 65 PM peak hour trips (30 northbound/35 southbound).
▪             Some of the traffic from neighborhoods and businesses along NE 10th Avenue and NE 149th
              Street that currently uses the NE 134th/139th Street interchange to access I-5 to/from the north
              may use the NE 179th Street interchange instead. To estimate the rerouted traffic demand,
              approximately 10% of the traffic using the northbound on-ramp on NE 139th Street and 15% of


\\grp.mck\data\users\rlb\PIM Working Files\deltekpim.mcknze.com\RPT-Clark County-Skyview Station TIS-180917 REV.docx   14
              the traffic using the southbound off-ramp on NE 134th Street was assumed to divert to the
              NE 179th Avenue interchange ramps. The southbound percentage was assumed to be higher
              because the travel time saving is greater than northbound. This assumption diverts 40 AM peak
              hour trips (15 northbound/25 southbound) and 55 PM peak hour trips (25 northbound/30
              southbound).
▪             Some of the traffic from the neighborhoods and businesses along NE 10th Avenue, NE 164th
              Street, and NE Delfel Road currently uses the NE 179th Street interchange to access I-5 and I-205
              to/from the south may use the NE 139th/134th Street interchange instead. To estimate the
              rerouted traffic demand, approximately 5% of the traffic using the NE 179th Street ramps to/from
              the south was assumed to divert to the I-5 and I-205 ramps at NE 139th Street or NE 134th Street.
              This assumption diverts 20 AM peak hour trips (5 northbound/15 southbound) and 30 PM peak
              hour trips (15 northbound/15 southbound).

Figure 7 presents the NE 10th Avenue traffic reroutes for the AM and PM peak hours. Appendix G includes
the supporting documentation.

A comparison of the PM peak hour rerouted traffic volumes using the diversion assumptions outlined
above and the difference between the 2018 No Build and Build scenarios from the Kittelson report shows
comparable results.

IV.           SITE DEVELOPMENT

The trip generation, distribution, and assignment for the proposed Skyview Station development are
described below.

Proposed Development

The proposed Skyview Station development will include approximately 80,150 square feet (SF) of
shopping center.

As shown in the attached plan, two site accesses are proposed:
▪             A full-movement driveway is proposed on NE 10th Avenue, a designated collector street. This
              driveway will be located opposite NE 141st Street and will include one inbound and two outbound
              travel lanes.
▪             A second limited access driveway is proposed on NE 139th Street, a designated minor arterial.
              This driveway will be limited to right-in/right-out (RIRO) movements only and will be aligned
              opposite the bus-only access serving the Salmon Creek Park & Ride.

As noted previously, a TRM will be submitted with the development application to add the site driveway
on NE 139th Street. Because the proposed RIRO has not been approved, traffic operations will be
evaluated both with and without it.

Generation Manual, 10th Edition. The pass-by trip rates are based on the ITE Trip Generation Handbook,
3rd Edition.

In accordance with Clark County’s Traffic Impact Fee (TIF) Program, the overall TIF for the Skyview Station

V.            SITE ACCESS AND CIRC ULATION

The evaluation of site access and on-site circulation includes the assessment of access spacing, sight
distance, and traffic warrants.

Site Access

As previously stated, the proposed development will provide access to the site via two site accesses:
▪             A full-movement driveway is proposed on NE 10th Avenue, a designated collector street. This
              driveway will be located opposite NE 141st Street and will include one inbound and two outbound
              travel lanes.
▪             A second limited access driveway is proposed on NE 139th Street, a designated minor arterial.
              This driveway will be limited to right-in/right-out (RIRO) movements only and will be aligned
              opposite the bus-only access serving the Salmon Creek Park & Ride.

Number of Accesses

The project is expected to generate 5,072 net daily driveway trips, including 1,760 pass-by trips and 3,312
primary trips. Per CCC 40.350.30(B)(4)(d)(1)(b), “the number of driveways and driveway lanes on arterials
shall be based upon an estimate of site traffic generation in accordance with Table 40.350.030-6.” This
table shows that sites generating more than 2,000 daily trips can have an additional driveway on a minor
arterial.

Access Sp acing

The proposed access on NE 10th Avenue will be aligned opposite NE 141st Street and the two accesses
serving the existing site uses (DeWitt Construction and a single-family residence) will be closed. Per CCC
Table 40.350.030-4, minimum separation for driveways on a collector with a 35-mph posted speed is 150
feet. The centerline of the proposed access is approximately 440 feet north of the stop bar at NE 139th
Street and approximately 150 south of the driveway for the single-family residence immediately north of
the site.

The proposed access on NE 139th Avenue will be aligned opposite the bus-only access serving the Salmon
Creek Park & Ride. Per CCC Table 40.350.030-4, minimum separation for driveways on an arterial with a
35-mph posted speed is also 150 feet. The centerline of the proposed access is approximately 390 feet
east of the stop bar at NE 10th Avenue and more than 1,000 feet west of the freeway ramps.

Both proposed accesses would meet the County spacing standards.

Sight Distance Evaluation

Sight distance for the proposed site accesses was evaluated based on CCC 40.350.030(B)(8). For a posted
speed of 35 mph, the stopping sight distance (SSD) shall be 250 feet and the intersection sight distance
(ISD) shall be 350 feet.

NE 10th Avenue is a straight roadway with clear SSD and ISD in both directions as measured 15 feet from
the edge of the vehicle travel lane. Landscaping along the site frontage will maintain the necessary sight
triangles.



\\grp.mck\data\users\rlb\PIM Working Files\deltekpim.mcknze.com\RPT-Clark County-Skyview Station TIS-180917 REV.docx   20
NE 139th Street has a slight curvature but the proposed right-out movement from the site will have clear
SSD and ISD looking to the west, as needed.

On-Site Circulation

Internal drive aisles will be constructed through the site connecting both the main driveway and proposed
RIRO with all parcels on the site. All site parking will be accessible via the drive aisles and will have access
to both proposed driveways.

Pedestrians will have two site access connections from NE 139th Street and one connection from NE 10th
Avenue.

Access Alternatives

If access on NE 139th Street is restricted to right-in movements only, traffic would have two options for
entering the site but only one option for exiting the site. Limiting the options for exiting vehicles would
concentrate all the exiting traffic at one location, which would result in longer on-site queues. Moreover,
should circumstances arise, such as a severe crash on NE 10th Avenue which could interfere with the
operations of the primary site access, no other access options would be available for exiting vehicles.

If no access is provided on NE 139th Street, then all entering and exiting traffic would be concentrated at
a single access point. This alternative would limit accessibility for emergency vehicles entering the site as
well as raising concerns for exiting vehicles.




\\grp.mck\data\users\rlb\PIM Working Files\deltekpim.mcknze.com\RPT-Clark County-Skyview Station TIS-180917 REV.docx   21
VI.           OPERATIONS ANALYSIS

Two aspects of operational analysis were evaluated for the study area intersections: 1) intersection
operation analysis, which evaluates how well an intersection processes traffic demand; and 2) queuing
analysis, which compares intersection queues with available storage for different travel lanes.

Intersection Operations Analysis

Intersection operations are generally measured by three mobility standards: volume-to-capacity (v/c)
ratio, level-of-service (LOS), and delay (measured in seconds). Signalized and all-way stop-controlled
(AWSC) intersections are measured by one overall v/c ratio, LOS, and delay. Two-way stop-controlled
(TWSC) intersections are typically measured by a single v/c ratio, LOS, and delay representative of the
worst stopped movement.

Perfo rmance Mea sures

Two jurisdictional standards apply in the study area. All intersections are under Clark County jurisdiction
except for the I-5 and I-205 interchange ramps.

Clark County

CCC Section 40.350.020(G) defines the mobility standards for County intersections as:
▪             LOS E at unsignalized intersections where signal warrants are not met
▪             LOS D at unsignalized intersections where signal warrants are met
▪             Delay for individual movements at signalized intersections equal to or less than two (2) cycle
              lengths or 240 seconds in delay (whichever is less)

WSDOT

WSDOT sets LOS standards for state highways based on RCW 47.06.140(2). The LOS standards are set
jointly by regional transportation planning organizations (RTPOs) and WSDOT for urban and rural
highways. The LOS standard for urban highways developed by the Regional Transportation Council (RTC)
and WSDOT in Clark County is LOS E.

Methodology

Intersection operations were analyzed with the use of Synchro 9 software, which utilizes the
Transportation Research Board’s Highway Capacity Manual (HCM) 2000 and 2010 methodologies. All
signalized study area intersections were reported using HCM 2000 and all unsignalized study area
intersections were reported using HCM 2010, per the City’s Traffic Study Guidelines. Signal timing
information was obtained from City, County, and WSDOT staff, and is presented in Appendix J.

Findings

Due to the size of the study area, the operations results are summarized by jurisdiction. Only the overall
intersection operation result for signalized intersections and the critical movement for unsignalized
intersections are presented in each jurisdiction table. The operation results summarized for each lane of
lane group are presented in summary tables in Appendix K and HCM reports are presented in Appendix L.

Access Alternatives

The site plan includes an access proposed on NE 139th Street with turns limited to right-in/right-out
movements. County approval of the proposed access is required; therefore, three access alternatives are
evaluated:
▪             No access on NE 139th Street; all traffic entering and exiting the site must use the access on
              NE 10th Avenue. (Note: This alternative is assumed in Table 6.)
▪             Right-in only, which would allow westbound rights from NE 139th Street into the site while all
              traffic would exit the site onto NE 10th Avenue.
▪             Right-in/Right-out, which would allow westbound rights from NE 139th Street into the site and
              southbound rights onto NE 139th Street out of the site.

At the intersection of NE 139th Street and NE 10th Avenue, both access alternatives improve overall
intersection operations compared with the no access alternative. However, the right-in access alternative
performs slightly better that than the RIRO because the shift in traffic volume demand is less favorable
for the critical movements that define the overall intersection performance. For example, some of the
exiting traffic would shift from the southbound right-turn lane on NE 10th Avenue, which is not a critical
movement, to the westbound through lanes on NE 139th Street, which are critical.

In summary, both the right-in and RIRO improve operations at intersections adjacent to the site, but the
RIRO provides an overall greater benefit by more substantially reducing traffic demand on NE 10th Avenue
and the full site access opposite NE 141st Street.

Intersection Queuing Analysis

An intersection queuing analysis was conducted for the six study area intersections during the AM and
PM peak hour to evaluate any potential queue spillbacks:
▪             NE 10th Avenue/NE 141st Street/Site Access
▪             NE 139th Street/NE 10th Avenue
▪             NE 139th Street/RIRO (Post-Development)
▪             NE 139th Street/I-5 SB On-Ramp
▪             NE 139th Street/I-5 NB Off-Ramp
▪             NE 139th Street/I-205 NB On-Ramp

These intersections either abut the site or were identified as a concern by WSDOT.

Methodology

Available queue storage lengths were estimated using Google Earth Pro software and rounded to the
nearest 5 feet. For turn lanes, two available storage values are stated: the first represents the striped
storage; and the second is the effective storage, or the length physically available regardless of striping,
such as a center turn lane upstream of a striped left-turn lane at an intersection. Although through travel



\\grp.mck\data\users\rlb\PIM Working Files\deltekpim.mcknze.com\RPT-Clark County-Skyview Station TIS-180917 REV.docx                                  26
lanes have no storage defined by striping, two values are reported for storage: the first is the distance to
an upstream driveway; the second is the distance to an upstream intersection.

The 95th percentile queues were estimated using SimTraffic software. Queue demand results were
rounded to the nearest 25 feet to represent average vehicle lengths.

Findings

The AM and PM peak hour 95th percentile queues are summarized by jurisdiction and only locations
where queue deficiencies are present or projected are summarized. Bold text indicates that the calculated
queue exceeds the storage for the travel lane. The SimTraffic output sheets are provided in Appendix M.

        Roadway Segment Analysis

        In addition to the intersection analysis, the County requires that roadway segments be analyzed to ensure
        they do not exceed the County’s standard.

        Perfo rmance Mea sures

        direction of travel.

        Methodology

        Capacity volumes are designated by the County for both urban and rural arterials and collectors and are
        presented in the CCC Table 40.350.020-1. The County’s Arterial Atlas was utilized to determine the County
        designation for all study area roadway segments. The directional segment volumes were then divided by
        the respective roadway capacities to determine the v/c ratios.

      All roadways currently meet and are anticipated to continue to meet the County’s capacity standard of
      0.90 or better under all development scenarios except for two segments:
      ▪             During the AM peak hour, the segment of NE Salmon Creek Avenue between NE 134th Street and
                    NE 50th Avenue is anticipated to have a v/c ratio of 1.08 in the eastbound direction under pre-
                    development conditions. The v/c ratio is not anticipated to change under post-development
                    conditions because the proposed Skyview Station will not add any new trips to this link in this
                    direction.
      ▪             During the PM peak hour, the segment of N 139th Street between the I-205 NB On-Ramp and
                    NE 20th Avenue is anticipated to have a v/c ratio of 0.91 in the westbound direction under pre-
                    development conditions and 0.94 under post development conditions. However, this segment is
                    not controlled by a traffic signal or STOP sign; thus, the capacity of the segment is underestimated
                    using the concurrency methodology. This segment has a free right-turn movement onto the
                    freeway ramp which more than 35% percent of the traffic uses. Once the traffic turns for the
                    highway, the v/c ratio for the next segment would drop below 0.60 for all conditions.

      In summary, neither segment listed above reflects a project impact that would trigger the need for
      mitigation. On NE Salmon Creek Avenue, the segment is over capacity under pre-development conditions
      and the proposed project does not change the v/c ratio of the link. On NE 139th Street, the arterial
      capacity assumption underestimates the capacity of this free-flow segment and capacity of the adjacent
      segment is well below the County’s v/c ratio threshold.

VII.          MITIGATION AND RECOMMENDATIONS

Operational concerns were identified at the site access on NE 10th Avenue. Potential mitigation measures
are discussed below, followed by recommendations.

Potential Mitigation Measures

To address operational and queuing concerns at the intersection of NE 10th Avenue at NE 141st
Street/Site Access, potential mitigation measures were considered.

Even with the traffic reductions at this intersection that could be realized with an access on NE 139th
Street, the westbound left-turn movement from the site is anticipated to be over capacity under post-
development conditions. Only one potential mitigation measure was considered at this intersection: a
traffic signal at the site access on NE 10th Avenue. A preliminary review of peak hour signal warrants
shows that the PM peak hour would meet the warrant threshold.

Table 14 summarizes intersection operations with these measures in place for all three access
alternatives. The traffic signal was assumed to have permitted phasing in the east-west direction and
protected/permitted phasing in the north-south direction. An actuated but uncoordinated cycle length of
90 seconds was assumed during both the AM and PM peak hours.

Installation of a traffic signal at the site access would greatly improve the operations for traffic leaving the
site, with relatively short delays for other traffic movements at the intersection.

Recommendations

The following recommendations improve study area operations:
▪             A traffic signal is recommended at the intersection of NE 141st Street/Site Access/NE 10th Avenue
              with development of Skyview Station to reduce delays and queuing.
▪             The proposed RIRO access on NE 139th Street is recommended for the following reasons:
              □             Site trip generation meets the County criteria for an additional driveway on a minor
                            arterial.
              □             The proposed location of the access on NE 139th Street will meet the driveway spacing
                            criteria for arterials.
              □             NE 139th Street is the only practical location for a second site access. A second access on
                            NE 10th Avenue would provide no operational benefits to either the site or the
                            surrounding transportation system.
              □             If no additional access is provided on NE 139th Street, then all entering and exiting traffic
                            would be concentrated at a single access point. Should circumstances arise, such as a
                            severe crash on NE 10th Avenue that interferes with the operations of the primary site
                            access, no other access options would be available.
              □             The RIRO provides additional access for emergency vehicles entering/exiting the site.
              □             Both the right-in and RIRO will reduce site traffic through the adjacent signalized
                            intersection at NE 139th Street and NE 10th Avenue but the RIRO provides a greater
                            reduction to traffic on NE 10th Avenue.
              □             Both the right-in and RIRO improve operations at intersections adjacent to the site but
                            the RIRO provides an overall greater benefit by more substantially reducing traffic
                            demand on NE 10th Avenue and the full site access opposite NE 141st Street.
              □             Both the right-in and RIRO reduce some queues at intersections adjacent to the site but
                            the RIRO provides an overall greater benefit by reducing traffic demand at the full site
                            access opposite NE 141st Street.

Mackenzie has prepared this scoping letter in advance of preparing the required Traffic Impact Study (TIS) for Phase 1 of
the Skyview Station development. This letter presents trip generation and distribution, analysis periods, and study area
recommendations.

SITE CONDITIONS

The site comprises two tax lots (property identification numbers 185726000 and 185727000) totaling 8.66 acres. Both lots
have existing development, but none will remain with the Skyview Station development.

The site is within the City of Vancouver Urban Growth Area but outside city limits. Clark County zoning is General
Commercial (GC)

PROJECT SUMMARY

Phase 1 of the proposed Skyview Station development will include approximately 80,150 square feet (SF) of shopping
center.

As shown in the attached plan, two site accesses are proposed:
▪         A full-movement driveway is proposed on NE 10th Avenue, a designated collector street. This driveway will be
          located opposite NE 141st Street and will include one inbound and two outbound travel lanes.
▪         A second limited access driveway is proposed on NE 139th Street, a designated minor arterial. This driveway will
          be limited to right-in/right-out (RIRO) movements only and will be aligned opposite the bus-only access serving
          the Salmon Creek Park & Ride.

A technical road modification will be submitted with the development application to add the site driveway on NE 139th
Street. Per Clark County Code (CCC) Table 40.350.030-6, an additional driveway may be allowed on a minor arterial for
sites generating more than 2,000 daily trips. The access will meet the driveway spacing criteria for arterials as outlined in
CCC Table 40.350.030-4. However, because the proposed RIRO has not been approved, traffic operations will be evaluated
both with and without it.

Site Trip Generation

Trip generation estimates were developed using the Institute of Transportation Engineers (ITE) Trip Generation Manual,
10th Edition. The pass-by trip rates are based on the ITE Trip Generation Handbook, 3rd Edition.

Table 1 summarizes the trip generation for the proposed development. The mixed retail estimates were prepared
assuming the “Shopping Center” (ITE Code 820) because the rates reflect the variety of retail and service uses that are
found in most shopping centers. This approach allows for more flexibility as the site develops and produces similar trip
generation results for the PM peak hour and daily estimates as an assessment of individual uses.

trips; and 66 AM peak hour, 158 PM peak hour, and 1,760 daily trips are pass-by trips.

To estimate the net site trip generation, the existing trips were subtracted from the trip generated by the proposed
Skyview Station development, as summarized in Table 3. The net primary trip generation is reduced to 114 AM peak hour,
296 PM peak hour, and 3,312 daily primary trips with the subtraction of existing trips while the pass-by volumes remain
unchanged.

TRIP DISTRIBUTION

Site trip distribution varies by trip type. The basis for distributing each trip type is calculated below.

Primary Trips

Site trip distribution for primary trips is based on the select zone base year (2010) and future year (2035) travel volumes
plots for Traffic Analysis Zone (TAZ) 95. Primary trip distribution for the AM and PM peak hour is assumed to be:
▪         20% to/from the north
          □      12% via I-5 using either NE 134th/NE 139th Street ramps or NE 10th Avenue to NE 179th Street ramps
          □      4% via NE 10th Avenue to NE Delfel Road north of NE 179th Street
          □      4% via NE 179th Street to areas east of the interchange
▪         57% to/from the south
          □      24% via I-5 split between the NE 134th and NE 139th Street ramps
          □      24% via I-205
          □      5% via NE Highway 99
          □      4% to/from residential areas south of NE Tenney Road/E 134th Street
▪         15% to/from the west
          □      10% via NE 139th Street
          □      5% via NE 149th Street
▪         8% to/from the east
          □       2% via NE 20th Avenue
          □       1% via NE 29th Avenue
          □       3% via NE Salmon Creek Avenue
          □       2% to/from residential areas along NE 139th Street and NE 134th Street

Pass-by Trips

Distribution for pass-by trips were estimated from the historical traffic count data on NE Fourth Plain Boulevard east of
NE Ward Road (2015 road tube data and 2013 intersection counts). The distributions are different for the AM and PM
peak hours to reflect difference in directional split between those two periods.

Pass-by trips trip distribution assumptions for the AM peak hour are:
▪         15% from northbound NE10th Avenue
▪         35% from southbound NE 10th Avenue
▪         25% from eastbound NE 139th Street
▪         25% from westbound NE 139th Street

Pass-by trips trip distribution assumptions for the PM peak hour are:
▪         25% from northbound NE10th Avenue
▪         25% from southbound NE 10th Avenue
▪         25% from eastbound NE 139th Street
▪         25% from westbound NE 139th Street

STUDY AREA

Per Clark County Code (CCC) 40.350.020, the study area may include intersections within 3 miles of the project site since
trip generation is estimated to be greater than 250 net new weekday PM peak hour trips (i.e., primary trips).

ANALYSIS YEARS & PERIODS

The TIS will review the AM and PM peak hour conditions at the study area intersections for the following scenarios:
▪         2018 Existing
▪         2020 Pre-Development without proposed development
▪         2020 Post-Development with proposed development

Pre-Development Assumptions

The pre-development conditions will reflect a build-out year scenario without the proposed development. This scenario
includes traffic from 2018 existing conditions, background traffic growth to year 2020, in-process traffic from other
approved developments that have not yet been constructed, and traffic reroutes from changes in the transportation
network.

Background Traffic Growth

An average 2% annual growth rate will be applied to existing 2018 traffic volumes over two years to estimate 2020
background traffic growth.

In-Process Traffic

The following in-process developments will be included in the pre-development condition based on information provided
by you:
▪         Vancouver Clinic at Salmon Creek
▪         Phase 1: 179th Street Commercial
▪         Phase 2: 179th Street Commercial
▪         iTech Prepatory School

Traffic Reroutes

Two Clark County TIP projects along NE 10th Avenue will fully connect NE 139th Street to NE 179th Street creating a local
parallel route to I-5 on the west side of the freeway. This improvement is anticipated to change some of the area travel
patterns when completed.

A Transportation Impact Discipline Report for the NE 10 Avenue (NE 154th to NE 164th Street) Project #370922 was
prepared by Kittelson & Associates, Inc. in June 2014. The report included analysis of No Build and Build conditions for an
opening year (2018) and a future year of 2035. Because the traffic data was collected prior to the opening of the NE 139th
Street interchange, the opening year analysis needed to estimate changes in travel patterns from the interchange
improvements as well as the NE 10th Avenue Project. Furthermore, the study only includes PM peak hour volumes and
did not address many of the intersection included the Skyview Station study area.

For these reasons, we propose to estimate the near-term traffic reroutes based on the 2018 existing traffic counts using
the following assumptions of changes traffic flow patterns:
▪         The NE 10th Avenue connection may provide a more direct route for to/from NE 179th Street than NW 11th
          Avenue. To estimate the rerouted traffic demand, approximately 20% of the traffic traveling east-west on
          NE 179th Street at NE Delfel Road was assumed to divert from NW 11th Avenue to NE 10th Avenue.
▪         Some of the traffic from neighborhoods and businesses along NE 10th Avenue and NE 149th Street that currently
          uses the NE 134th/139th Street interchange to access I-5 to/from the north may use the NE 179th Street
          interchange instead. To estimate the rerouted traffic demand, approximately 10% of the traffic using the
          northbound on-ramp on NE 139th Street and 15% of the traffic using the southbound off-ramp on NE 134th Street
          was assumed to divert to the NE 179th Avenue interchange ramps. The southbound percentage was assumed to
          be higher because the travel time saving is greater than northbound.
▪         Some of the traffic from the neighborhoods and businesses along NE 10th Avenue, NE 164th Street, and NE Delfel
          Road the currently uses the NE 179th Street interchange to access I-5 and I-205 to/from the south may use the
          NE 139th/134th Street interchange instead. To estimate the rerouted traffic demand, approximately 5% of the
          traffic using the NE 179th Street ramps to/from the south was assumed to divert to the I-5 and I-205 ramps at
          NE 139th Street or NE 134th Street.

Comparison of the resulting PM peak hour traffic reroute volumes using the diversion assumptions outlined above and

Proposed Development Plan
Three Creeks Investors, LLC is proposing to develop the first 60,000 square feet of a 545,000 square
foot integrated commercial development. Phase 1 site access is proposed via two driveways, a right-
in/right-out driveway on NE 15th Avenue and a driveway connecting with a new full movement
roadway located on the east side of NE 15th Avenue. Completion of site construction and occupancy of
the development is anticipated in 2014 or 2015.


Trip Generation
A trip generation estimate was prepared for the proposed development based on information provided
in the standard reference manual, Trip Generation, 9th Edition, published by the Institute of
Transportation Engineers (ITE, Reference 2). The pass-by and diverted trip rates were also determined
based on ITE’s Trip Generation, 9th Edition. Based on the proposed development plan, ITE Land Use
Code 820 (Shopping Center) was selected to estimate trips associated with the proposed development.
Table 5 summarizes the daily, weekday a.m. and p.m. peak hour trips expected for the proposed
development (daily trips have been rounded to the nearest ten).

Table 5 - Trip Generation Estimate

                                                                            Weekday AM Peak Hour    Weekday PM Peak Hour
                                                                  Weekday
             Land Use                ITE Code    Size (Sq. Ft.)

Trip Distribution/Assignment
The site-generated trips shown in Table 3 were distributed onto the study area roadways based on a
Select Zone Assignment prepared by the Southwest Washington Regional Transportation Council, a
market study for the site, as well as the location of major trip origins and destinations in Clark County.
Figure 8 illustrates the trip distribution pattern. Based on the trip distribution pattern, Figures 9 and 10
show the assignment of site-generated trips at the study intersections during the weekday a.m. and
weekday p.m. peak hours, respectively.

Per prior approvals from County staff, approximately 50 percent of all diverted trips were assumed to
be traveling south along I-5 and 50 percent were assumed to be traveling north along I-5. In addition,
given the relatively low traffic volumes along NE 179th Avenue and NE 15th Avenue, approximately 70
percent of pass-by trips were assumed to be associated with I-5, of which approximately 50 percent
were assumed to be traveling south along I-5 and 50 percent were assumed to be traveling north.
Figures F-1 through F-6 in Appendix “F” illustrate the net new, pass-by, and diverted trips at the study
intersections during the weekday a.m. and weekday p.m. peak hours, respectively.

iTech Preparatory School                                                            Revised Traffic Impact Analysis


The appropriateness of using ITE school trip generation rates for the analysis in this TIA was reviewed to
determine applicability for a magnet school such as iTech Prep. This research identified that both the
Middle School and High School rates published in ITE’s Trip Generation manual include both public and
private schools as the primary data source. Studies of both rates also conclude that using head count
students as the independent variable is preferred. The use of school buses varied considerably.
     •    High school trip generation rates are based on studies from the 1960’s through the 2000’s, and
          include data from a charter school. For the AM and PM peak periods, the high school trip
          generation rates rely on at least 40 studies (75 during the AM peak and 40 for the PM peak)
     •    For middle schools the data is more recent and includes studies only from the 1990’s to current
          times. Trip generation rates for middle schools rely on 25 studies during the AM peak and 15
          studies for the PM peak.
No specific data was available online for magnet schools. However, the fact that the ITE rates for high
schools are based on a large number of studies and include both private and charter schools make these
seem reasonable for use on the iTech Prep site. Also, the high school rate assumes a decent amount of
school bus ridership. Middle school rates are also a mix of public and private schools and seem
applicable to the iTech Prep facility.
The total trip generation expected from this project was calculated by applying the unit measure for
each land use category (total head count students) to the appropriate trip generation rate. The trip
generation estimate for the iTech Prep School is shown in Table 14. This table reflects both the total trip
generation expected for the project, as well as the net new trips that would be added through the
expansion and relocation of the existing facility. Total trip generation will be used to assess localized
traffic operations including the project’s driveways. Net trip generation will be used to assess any
potential impacts on the areawide transportation system, particularly along the NE 134th Street corridor.
